title: Are the girls taller than the boys in this class?
description: A Grade 5 class's heights are compared by mean and median on the board, and the students above the class mean are counted. Keeko doubts that every girl must be taller than every boy.
teaching_notes: One idea: a higher mean says the group is taller on the whole, not that every member is. The book prints 144.4 for the class mean; the data gives 4046 ÷ 28 = 144.5, and the count above the mean is the same for both. Watch for children who read a group average as a rule for everyone.

source: A Grade 5 class has 17 boys and 11 girls with the heights in
video_script.why: The child can find a mean and median and now compares two groups inside one class.
video_script.substitution: Comparing means and medians tells us about the groups; individuals must be read from the dots.
video_script.wrong_answer: every girl is taller than every boy
video_script.wrong_move: turns a higher mean for the girls into every girl being taller, although the tallest and the shortest students are both boys
video_script.payoff_line: Girls are taller on the whole, but not every girl

final_answer.value: Girls are taller on the whole (mean 146.91 against 142.94); 15 students, 8 of them boys, are taller than the class mean of 144.5 cm
final_answer.spoken: girls are taller on the whole, but not every girl; fifteen students, eight of them boys, are taller than the class mean

hold_back: Girls are taller on the whole, but not every girl
maths_rules: boys: total 2430, mean 142.94 cm (to two places), median 144 cm (9th of 17), 128 to 158
girls: total 1616, mean 146.91 cm (to two places), median 148 cm (6th of 11), 136 to 156
class: 4046 / 28 = 144.5 cm (the book prints 144.4), median 145 cm
no height lies between 144.4 and 144.5, so the count is the same
video_script.design: One idea: group averages against individuals. Two dot plots, boys above and girls below, stay on the board; a mean line sweeps across the class.

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, find the mean of each group.
<bookmark mark='s2'/>The boys' heights add up to two thousand four hundred and thirty.
<bookmark mark='s3'/>Divided by seventeen, their mean is about one hundred and forty two point nine four.
<bookmark mark='s4'/>The girls' heights add up to one thousand six hundred and sixteen.
<bookmark mark='s5'/>Divided by eleven, their mean is about one hundred and forty six point nine one.

The girls have the higher mean and the higher median.

<bookmark mark='e2'/>All twenty eight heights add up to four thousand and forty six.

<bookmark mark='e4'/>Your book shows one hundred and forty four point four. The count below is the same either way.

beats.on_screen: Answer: girls are taller on the whole, but not every girl; 15 students, 8 of them boys, are taller than the class mean of 144.5 cm
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Girls are taller on the whole, but not every girl.
Fifteen students are taller than the class mean, and eight of them are boys.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks every girl is taller than every boy, because the girls' mean is higher.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The tallest student, one hundred and fifty eight centimetres, is a boy.
The shortest student, one hundred and twenty eight centimetres, is also a boy.
<bookmark mark='idea'/>A higher mean speaks for the group, not for each child.
